TEMPORARY DESIGN FIXTURE: OpenMail / JMAP / OpenSMTPD

Status: illustrative managed-blob storage option, not the Maildir layout.
See openmail/BACKENDS.txt for the current three-source plan and openmail/DESIGN.txt
for daemon implementation status. SQL backend integration, installer, LMTP
listener, and setup UI are not implemented by these fixtures.
All addresses and message content are synthetic.

Design principles: KISS and a focused mail domain
------------------------------------------------
OpenMail does one job: provide reliable mailbox access and a web interface
through JMAP. OpenSMTPD remains responsible for SMTP transport, queueing, retries,
and relay policy. Follow OpenSMTPD's emphasis on simple configuration, clear
interfaces, small components, and least privilege; this is an independent
project, not an OpenSMTPD component or endorsement.

Keep the first implementation small:
- One OpenMail executable and one rc.d service; serve built web assets directly.
- SQLite and private local message files first; no database abstraction until
  a second backend is needed. PostgreSQL/MariaDB examples below are future design.
- One delivery interface: private LMTP from OpenSMTPD. One client protocol: JMAP.
- Stable IDs, transactional changes, durable delivery, and recovery are core
  requirements; simplicity must preserve those guarantees.
- Use base OpenBSD facilities for service control, HTTPS proxying, and logging.
- Keep configuration explicit, errors actionable, and dependencies reviewed.
- Validate mailbox behavior before adding features; advertise only implemented
  JMAP capabilities and verify protocol conformance.

OpenMail does not implement an SMTP transport, its own retry queue, IMAP,
POP3, DNS management, certificate issuance, antivirus, calendars, or a plugin
framework. Compose with existing tools for those responsibilities.
The setup UI configures OpenMail and exports a small OpenSMTPD configuration
fragment for operator review. Start with documented local install steps rather
than building a general system configuration manager or privileged web backend.
The installer mentioned below is a future scoped packaging step.

Web service and OpenBSD lifecycle
--------------------------------
OpenMail is a persistent web daemon written in Rust managed through rcctl. One
binary serves the browser UI, authenticated setup/admin routes, and JMAP API.
It also provides a separate private LMTP listener for OpenSMTPD delivery.
PHP-FPM and a separate frontend runtime are not needed for this proposed app;
built frontend assets are served by the Rust HTTP server.

Project name: OpenMail. Executable and service name: openmail (not installed yet).
Proposed binary: /usr/local/bin/openmail
Proposed configuration: /etc/openmail/config.toml
Proposed service script: /etc/rc.d/openmail
Run as a dedicated unprivileged account, with access to its private storage.
The rc.d script must support the binary's foreground/background behavior.

Example operator commands AFTER implementing and installing that service:
  rcctl enable openmail
  rcctl start openmail
  rcctl check openmail
  rcctl restart openmail
  rcctl stop openmail

Listen address and port are configuration options. Proposed initial default:
  http_listen = "127.0.0.1:8080"
  lmtp_socket = "/var/run/openmail/lmtp.sock"

An operator on the host can open http://127.0.0.1:8080/; remote setup can use
an SSH tunnel. Production browsers connect via HTTPS through relayd to this
HTTP listener. A configured non-loopback bind permits direct network access;
require HTTPS at the application or trusted proxy before remote credential use.
LMTP is separate from the web port, with socket permissions allowing only the
delivery service and application accounts. Keep all mail data outside web roots.

First start serves a setup wizard until configured; require a locally generated
one-time setup token before accepting settings. After setup, disable bootstrap
access and require an authenticated administrator for configuration changes.
Database/storage credentials are stored in a protected server configuration.
The web daemon can manage application data and produce system config previews;
rcctl startup does not give it permission to edit OpenSMTPD system files.
Apply those changes through the local installer described below.
If the mailbox service is unavailable, OpenSMTPD queues/retries delivery; database
lookup failures must produce temporary failures rather than unknown-user replies.

Setup flow proposed for the future UI
-----------------------------------
1. Start with SQLite on one host. PostgreSQL/MariaDB remain future options.
2. Select a new database or connect to an existing one; review migrations.
3. Configure domains, virtual accounts, aliases, storage root, and quotas.
4. Generate OpenSMTPD SQL lookup configuration and LMTP delivery configuration.
5. Preview configuration changes and validate on the target OpenBSD release.
6. A local privileged installer applies system configuration and starts services.
7. Check recipient lookup, unknown-recipient rejection, delivery, JMAP sync,
   authenticated sending, and absence of unintended relay permissions.

The browser must not run as root or execute arbitrary supplied commands. Setup
should export configuration or invoke a narrowly scoped local installer. Never
expose database credentials or server filesystem paths in ordinary mail UI/API
responses. Existing OpenSMTPD configuration needs a merge, backup, and rollback.

Service boundaries
------------------
OpenSMTPD -> SQL directory lookup: domains, valid recipients, aliases, credentials
OpenSMTPD -> OpenMail LMTP listener: message envelope and original message bytes
OpenMail -> SQL mailbox records: IDs, memberships, keywords, quotas, sync journal
OpenMail -> private local files: immutable original messages
Browser  -> OpenMail JMAP API over HTTPS
OpenMail -> OpenSMTPD submission: outgoing mail

SQL table helpers are additional OpenSMTPD components. Verify package/backend
availability on the target release. MariaDB requires verification with the MySQL
helper. SMTP authentication hashes must match the selected helper's expectations;
web authentication and SMTP credentials need not share a password-hash format.

With PostgreSQL/MariaDB, use a restricted lookup role for OpenSMTPD and an app
role for OpenMail; mailbox tables must not be writable by the lookup role.
With SQLite, use a separate directory.sqlite and mailbox.sqlite to isolate file
access. OpenMail manages provisioning changes in directory.sqlite.
Separate SQLite files do not give one atomic transaction across provisioning
and mailbox state; create accounts disabled, provision, then enable routing.

Proposed private runtime layout (paths illustrative)
--------------------------------------------------
/var/mail/openmail/
  directory.sqlite                 SQLite directory, if selected
  mailbox.sqlite                   SQLite mailbox state, if selected
  staging/                         incomplete deliveries; never served
  accounts/<account-id>/blobs/
    <first-two-hash-characters>/<sha256>.eml

For PostgreSQL/MariaDB, database files are managed by that database server;
message files still live under this storage root. Account IDs are internally
generated; never use an unvalidated recipient address as a filesystem path.

This draft uses immutable .eml blobs, not a Maildir directory tree. SQL owns
folder memberships. Existing Maildir would need an importer; continued external
Maildir modifications would require a separate reconciliation design.

What is included here
---------------------
database-records.json       logical rows for one account and one received email
accounts/acct_demo/blobs/   an actual RFC 5322/MIME .eml file with an attachment

The blob row records the real SHA-256, relative file path, and byte length.
Attachments remain inside the original MIME message; separate decoded files
are optional caches. APIs may expose attachment blob IDs backed by MIME parts.
JSON here illustrates DB contents; it is not the message storage format.

Identity and sync rules
-----------------------
email_demo identifies the account's Email object permanently. blob_demo points
to its immutable bytes. message_id_header is sender-controlled metadata.
An SQL primary key (encoded as a valid JMAP ID) or generated opaque ID works.
Never regenerate or reuse public IDs, including after restore or migration.
Hash-based storage keys are internal, account-scoped, and not access tokens.

Move to Archive: replace Inbox membership with Archive membership; retain the
Email/blob IDs; commit an Email updated event with the new state.
Mark read: add the $seen keyword and commit another updated event.
Destroy: remove the Email and memberships; retain a destroyed event/tombstone.
Garbage-collect bytes only when no live reference or pending operation needs them.
Enforce account-scoped foreign keys and ownership checks on all memberships.

Every visible mutation and its sync event/state update must commit together.
Serialize state allocation per account so sequence ordering matches commits;
an ordinary global auto-increment counter alone is insufficient.
Clients use opaque state tokens derived from committed state. Expired change
history requires JMAP cannotCalculateChanges and a client resync.
Mailbox and Thread changes also need type-specific tracking in the real service;
the JSON shows only one Email creation, not a complete JMAP implementation.

Durable delivery and recovery
-----------------------------
Write bytes to staging, flush, atomically publish on the same filesystem, and
flush the destination directory as required. Commit mailbox rows, quota usage,
and sync events transactionally before acknowledging LMTP success per recipient.
Never commit a readable Email referencing an incomplete file.
Use recovery records and delayed garbage collection for interrupted deliveries
and orphaned blobs; filesystem and SQL writes are not one atomic transaction.
Use temporary delivery failures when durable acceptance is impossible.
If acknowledgement is lost after commit, SMTP/LMTP retry can deliver a duplicate;
do not claim exactly-once delivery or deduplicate solely by Message-ID/content.
Back up authoritative IDs, journal/state, directory data, and blobs consistently.
Search indexes and decoded attachment caches may be rebuilt; IDs must survive.
